title: Mul Naengmyeon
subtitle: Cold buckwheat noodles in chilled beef broth
excerpt: Chewy buckwheat noodles are served in an ice-cold, lightly seasoned beef broth topped with pickled radish, julienned cucumber, half a hard-boiled egg and a dab of sharp mustard. This recipe serves 2 and requires the broth to be made and chilled in advance, so allow at least 2 hours of chilling time on top of the 50 minutes of active work. It is Korea's most iconic summer dish.
sourceNotes: Naengmyeon originated in the Pyongyang region of what is now North Korea, where cold winters and the buckwheat-growing climate made cold noodles a natural food tradition. The dish travelled south and became beloved across Korea, particularly in summer. The Pyongyang style uses a clean, lightly flavoured meat broth while the Hamhung style uses a spicier sauce instead.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The broth can be made up to 2 days ahead and kept in the fridge. Add ice cubes to each bowl just before serving to ensure the broth is cold enough.

glossaryTerms.definition: Naengmyeon means cold noodles in Korean, combining 'naeng' (cold) and 'myeon' (noodles). The dish originated in the Pyongyang region of northern Korea and is traditionally eaten in summer. There are two main styles: mul naengmyeon, which uses a clear cold broth, and bibim naengmyeon, which uses a spicy gochujang sauce. The noodles are made from buckwheat and have a distinctively chewy, slightly dense texture.

Mul simply means water or broth in Korean. In the context of naengmyeon, it distinguishes the clear cold broth version from the spicy bibim version. The mul for naengmyeon is a seasoned beef broth that is chilled until very cold, sometimes with ice added directly to the bowl before serving. The broth should taste clean, slightly sweet and gently savoury.

Korean tradition holds that naengmyeon noodles should be cut with scissors at the table or just before serving, as their length symbolises long life. In restaurants a pair of scissors is brought out with the bowl. At home, cut them once or twice if the long strands make them difficult to eat.

content.text: Make the broth. Place the beef in a saucepan with the water. Bring to the boil, skim the foam, then reduce to a simmer. Cook for 20 minutes until the beef is cooked through. Remove the beef and set aside.

Stir the soy sauce, rice vinegar and sugar into the warm broth. Taste and adjust. The broth should be gently savoury, slightly sweet and lightly tart. Transfer to a container and refrigerate for at least 2 hours until thoroughly cold.
When the beef has cooled, slice it thinly against the grain. Lightly pickle the radish slices with a pinch each of salt and sugar and set aside for 10 minutes.

Cook the buckwheat noodles according to the packet instructions. Drain and rinse under cold running water until the noodles are completely cold, rubbing them together briefly to remove surface starch. Drain well.
Divide the noodles between two deep bowls. Arrange the sliced beef, pickled radish, julienned cucumber and halved eggs on top.
Add a few ice cubes to the cold broth, then ladle it over the noodles and toppings. Add a small dab of mustard and a scatter of sesame seeds. Serve immediately with scissors for cutting the noodles.

items.cause: They were not rinsed and rubbed under cold water immediately after draining
items.fix: Rinse buckwheat noodles very thoroughly under cold running water as soon as they are drained, rubbing them between your hands to separate the strands and remove surface starch. Keep them in a little cold water if not assembling immediately.

items.symptom: Broth tastes too sharp and vinegary
items.cause: Too much rice vinegar was added relative to the other seasonings
items.fix: Add a little more sugar and a splash of soy sauce to balance. The broth should be balanced between savoury, sweet and tart, with no single note dominating.

items.symptom: The dish does not feel cold enough to eat as naengmyeon should
items.cause: The broth was not chilled for long enough, or the noodles were still slightly warm
items.fix: Add extra ice cubes directly to the bowl just before serving. Make sure both the noodles and all toppings are fully cold before assembling.

content.text: Mul naengmyeon is the dish Koreans crave in the height of summer. In Seoul, specialist naengmyeon restaurants fill up in July and August with queues stretching out of the door. The bowl arrives with ice still floating in the broth. The noodles are chewy and dense in a way that no other noodle quite matches. It originated in the Pyongyang tradition of North Korea and carries a cultural weight beyond its ingredients.
